title: How an Artery Learned to Relax

scenes.tts: What relaxes an artery? In 1980, Robert Furgott and John Zawadzki mounted rings of rabbit aorta in an organ bath. Some rings kept their endothelium, the single layer of cells that lines the vessel. In others, it had been rubbed off.
scenes.visual: Question on top. An organ bath appears holding two rings of vessel wall. The left ring gains a thin blue lining; the right ring has none, labelled lining rubbed off.
scenes.narration: What relaxes an artery? In 1980, Robert Furchgott and John Zawadzki mounted rings of rabbit aorta in an organ bath. Some rings kept their endothelium, the single layer of cells that lines the vessel. In others, it had been rubbed off.
scenes.caption: What relaxes an artery? In 1980, Robert Furchgott and John Zawadzki mounted rings of rabbit aorta in an organ bath. Some rings kept their endothelium, the single layer of cells that lines the vessel. In others, it had been rubbed off.

scenes.tts: They added acetylcholine. It relaxed the intact rings but not the rubbed ones. So the lining was sending something to the muscle beneath it. That something lasted only seconds. In 1986, Furgott proposed that it is the gas nitric oxide, N O. Ignarro independently proposed the same.
scenes.caption: They added acetylcholine. It relaxed the intact rings but not the rubbed ones. So the lining was sending something to the muscle beneath it. That something lasted only seconds. In 1986, Furchgott proposed that it is the gas nitric oxide, NO. Ignarro independently proposed the same.
scenes.visual: Acetylcholine drops onto both rings. The intact ring widens; the rubbed ring does not. The rings give way to two layers, lining above muscle, with a question mark between them that becomes NO, credited to Furchgott 1986 and Ignarro.
scenes.narration: They added acetylcholine. It relaxed the intact rings but not the rubbed ones. So the lining was sending something to the muscle beneath it. That something lasted only seconds. In 1986, Furchgott proposed that it is the gas nitric oxide, NO. Ignarro independently proposed the same.

scenes.tts: Acetylcholine binds a G P C R on the endothelial cell, and calcium rises. Calcium, bound to calmodulin, switches on nitric oxide synthase. It makes N O from the amino acid arginine. N O is small and uncharged, so it crosses membranes freely. It cannot be aimed, and it reacts away within seconds. So only near neighbors receive it.
scenes.caption: Acetylcholine binds a GPCR on the endothelial cell, and calcium rises. Calcium, bound to calmodulin, switches on nitric oxide synthase. It makes NO from the amino acid arginine. NO is small and uncharged, so it crosses membranes freely. It cannot be aimed, and it reacts away within seconds. So only near neighbors receive it.
scenes.visual: Inside the endothelial cell a chain builds left to right: acetylcholine on a GPCR, calcium, calcium with calmodulin, nitric oxide synthase switching on, arginine in, NO dots out. Some dots cross to the muscle cell below; others fade away.
scenes.narration: Acetylcholine binds a GPCR on the endothelial cell, and calcium rises. Calcium, bound to calmodulin, switches on nitric oxide synthase. It makes NO from the amino acid arginine. NO is small and uncharged, so it crosses membranes freely. It cannot be aimed, and it reacts away within seconds. So only near neighbors receive it.

scenes.tts: In the muscle cell, N O binds the iron of a heme group in soluble guanylyl cyclase. It changes shape and makes c G M P from G T P. The c G M P switches on protein kinase G. The muscle relaxes, and the vessel widens. A phosphodiesterase, P D E five, ends the signal. Outside the eye, c G M P carries its signal by rising.
scenes.caption: In the muscle cell, NO binds the iron of a heme group in soluble guanylyl cyclase. It changes shape and makes cGMP from GTP. The cGMP switches on protein kinase G. The muscle relaxes, and the vessel widens. A phosphodiesterase, PDE5, ends the signal. Outside the eye, cGMP carries its signal by rising.
scenes.visual: In the muscle cell NO attaches to the heme of soluble guanylyl cyclase, which turns green and makes cGMP from GTP. cGMP switches on protein kinase G, and the walls of an idealised artery move apart. PDE5 destroys cGMP; then a rising arrow shows the signal is a rise.
